Science.contentMarkdown:
**Grade-level scope:** NYS writes middle-school science standards for Grades 6–8 as a band, not as a separate Grade 7 course sequence. This week supports MS-PS4-2: use models to describe how light and mechanical waves are reflected, absorbed, or transmitted through different materials. The standard limits assessment to qualitative applications; students explain what a model shows and use observed evidence rather than calculate wave behavior. This is grade-band support, not proof that Ditmas teaches the topic now. [New York State Middle School Science Learning Standards](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/standards-instruction/ms-science-learning-standards.pdf), MS-PS4-2.

**Sources:** NASA explains light reflecting, being absorbed, and passing through materials, and gives a pavement example. USGS compares recordings from the same earthquake at two nearby stations on different rock types. These are real source examples; any flashlight or rope test below is a new student investigation, not a reported result from NASA, USGS, or Ditmas. [NASA: Wave Behaviors](https://science.nasa.gov/ems/03_behaviors/); [NASA: Interactions Between Light and Matter](https://science.nasa.gov/asset/webb/interactions-between-light-and-matter/); [USGS: Rock Type Effects](https://earthquake.usgs.gov/education/listen/rocktype.php).

![NASA diagram of light interacting with matter](https://assets.science.nasa.gov/dynamicimage/assets/science/missions/webb/outreach/migrated/2021/STScI-01F8QMDJYFNQ2XS4BVC3GPAF76.png?w=1501&h=445&fit=clip&crop=faces%2Cfocalpoint)

*NASA's diagram gives real examples of light being reflected, absorbed, or transmitted, along with other behaviors. This week's target is reflection, absorption, and transmission. Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, and Leah Hustak/STScI; [NASA image source](https://science.nasa.gov/asset/webb/interactions-between-light-and-matter/).*

![USGS cartoon comparing seismic-wave paths through soft sand and hard rock](https://earthquake.usgs.gov/education/listen/images/rock-type.gif)

*USGS model of rock-type effects. The image is a cartoon, not a measured map of a particular earthquake. Read the source page and seismogram/audio comparison for the actual evidence. [USGS Rock Type Effects](https://earthquake.usgs.gov/education/listen/rocktype.php).*

#### Read: a material can reflect, absorb, and transmit a wave

When a wave reaches a material, some of its energy may **reflect** (bounce back), **transmit** (pass through), or be **absorbed** (taken into the material). A material does not have to do only one of these things. The result depends on the kind of wave, the material, and—in the case of light—the wavelength or color. NASA notes that a mirror reflects almost all of the light that reaches its smooth surface. Clear glass may transmit light while also reflecting a small part from its surface. A dark surface may absorb more light than a pale one.

NASA gives a real surface example: black pavement absorbs most of the visible and ultraviolet light that reaches it and reflects little, while light-colored concrete reflects more energy than it absorbs. When absorbed light makes molecules move and vibrate more, the material becomes warmer. This explains why the dark pavement can become hotter than the lighter sidewalk in strong sunlight. It does not mean all dark objects are hotter in every setting; the light source, exposure, surface, and conditions matter. [NASA: Wave Behaviors, Reflection and Absorption](https://science.nasa.gov/ems/03_behaviors/).

The same three words can describe mechanical waves, such as sound or seismic waves, but do not assume a sound wave behaves exactly like visible light. A rope pulse can reflect from a fixed end. Sound can reflect as an echo. Mechanical waves also travel through matter, and their energy can change as they pass through different materials.

USGS describes an example using one earthquake and two seismometers about five miles from it. One was on very solid rock; the other was in a fault zone. USGS says solid granite transmits energy better than broken-up fault-zone rock, where waves lose more energy—especially at higher frequencies. The page provides two seismograms and lets students listen to the recordings. It says the volume was adjusted to the same level, so students should compare the pitch and record shapes described by the source, not decide which site had a louder earthquake. The recordings are evidence that the material along a wave's path matters; this source does not isolate every cause of the difference. [USGS: Rock Type Effects](https://earthquake.usgs.gov/education/listen/rocktype.php).

#### Five study sessions — about 55–65 minutes each

| Session | Work | Evidence to save |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Learn the three interactions | Read the NASA source and the passage above. Use the NASA diagram to point out an example each of reflection, absorption, and transmission. Explain why the same material may reflect some incoming light and transmit or absorb other light. | A three-column glossary with one source example for each interaction. |
| 2 — Test light with safe materials | With an adult, shine a low-power flashlight at a plane mirror and use a white card to observe a reflected beam. Then compare how much light reaches a card behind clear plastic, wax paper, and cardboard. Keep the flashlight, distance, angle, background, and card position fixed; change only the sample. Do not look into the beam or use a laser. Record actual observations, not expected results. | A labeled setup sketch, predictions, observation table, and one note about what the simple test cannot measure. |
| 3 — Study a mechanical-wave model | Send one gentle pulse down a rope or spring toward a fixed end; observe whether a pulse returns. If equipment is unavailable, use the reflection model in the NYS standard and leave the observation table blank. Explain how this model is different from USGS seismic waves traveling through rock. | A before/after sketch showing incoming and reflected pulse directions, plus a model-limit note. |
| 4 — Read the USGS rock comparison | Open the USGS Rock Type Effects page. Record its comparison: same earthquake, stations about five miles away, different ground materials. Listen to the two linked records if audio works; follow the page's note that the volume was adjusted equally and compare pitch. Write which material USGS says transmits energy better and what the source says about energy loss in the fault zone. | A source table with matching conditions, changed condition, source observation, and a limit. |
| 5 — Explain with evidence | Complete the practice questions. Then write a claim about how materials affect a wave. Use one NASA light example and one USGS mechanical-wave example. State that the examples are different wave types and do not prove that every material behaves the same way. | A two-source claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph and corrected question set. |

18. They came from the **same earthquake** and were each **about five miles away**; the ground material/site differed (solid rock versus fault zone). The source's volume adjustment is another stated control for listening, not evidence that the two sites had the same original shaking.
19. USGS describes **this comparison** and states that rock type affects energy loss. It does not test every rock, earthquake, distance, instrument, or wave path.
20. **Answers vary.** A strong response uses an accurate NASA light example (mirror reflection, pavement absorption, or material transmission) and an accurate USGS rock example (different transmission/energy loss). It says those are different wave/material cases and does not overgeneralize.

Math.title: Use a scale drawing to find real dimensions
Math.subject: Math
Math.instructions: Work through the scale examples before solving. Convert each side first; find area only after both actual side lengths are known.
Math.explanation: A scale tells how a drawing length relates to a real length. If 1 inch represents 1.75 feet, multiply every drawing measurement by 1.75 to find the actual measurement. An 8-inch by 6-inch drawing represents 14 feet by 10.5 feet. The actual area is 14 × 10.5 = 147 square feet. Do not multiply the drawing’s area by the scale only once; both side lengths change.

English.title: Connect a claim to evidence
English.subject: English
English.instructions: This is an original practice scenario with made-up sample data. Read carefully, then distinguish the claim from the evidence.
English.passage: In a practice scenario, a student group compares two small sidewalk plots on the same sunny afternoon. The plot under a tree measures 28°C at the surface. The nearby plot without shade measures 34°C. The group writes, “The shaded plot was cooler during our measurement.” The two readings support that limited claim. They do not prove that every shaded place is always cooler, because the group measured only two plots once. A careful writer states what the evidence supports and avoids claiming more than the evidence can show.

Science.title: Model a convergent plate boundary
Science.subject: Science
Science.instructions: Read the passage and compare the world map with the cross-section model. The cross-section is schematic and not to scale.
Science.passage: Earth’s outer rigid layer is divided into large plates that move slowly relative to one another. Where two plates move toward each other, they meet at a convergent boundary. In some places, a denser oceanic plate bends and sinks beneath another plate. This process is called subduction. It can be associated with earthquakes and volcanic activity, but the details vary by boundary. A map helps show broad plate locations; a cross-section model shows a possible process beneath the surface. Neither drawing is a photograph of the mantle.

Social Studies.subject: Social Studies
Social Studies.instructions: Read the short background and inspect the painting as a source. Do not treat the painting as a photograph or as a complete record of every viewpoint.
Social Studies.passage: During the American Revolution, people held different views about independence. Patriots supported breaking from British rule. Loyalists wanted to remain connected to the British Crown. Some people tried to stay neutral, and many people’s choices were shaped by family, safety, community, and personal circumstances. These labels are a starting point, not a full explanation of any person’s beliefs. John Trumbull painted a scene connected to the Declaration of Independence in 1819, decades after the events shown. The painting is a later interpretation, so historians compare it with other sources and ask what it leaves out.

- **Constitution:** distinguish what a source says about the new government's design from later interpretation of its effects.
- **Expansion and reform:** track the period and point of view in each source; include the experiences and agency of people affected by expansion.
- **Nation divided:** compare primary-source claims with evidence and note the author/audience/context.

## Science

New York’s science standards specify a **Grades 6–8 middle-school band**, not a separate mandated Grade 7 textbook sequence. Grade 7’s local course may focus on selected units within the band. The official band includes physical science (matter, forces/motion, energy, waves), life science (cells, inheritance, ecosystems, natural selection), Earth/space science (Earth systems, weather/climate, geologic change, space), and engineering design. This is state content, not a claim that Ditmas teaches a specific Amplify unit in Grade 7.

The real Grade 8 NYS science test is a later middle-school check, not a Grade 7 textbook. [NYS P–12 Science Learning Standards](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/curriculum-instruction/p-12-science-learning-standards.pdf); [NYSED science standards and middle-grade resources](https://www.nysed.gov/state-assessment/nys-grades-3-8-science-learning-standards).

### How to build a science explanation from evidence

For any unit in the Grades 6–8 band, keep a three-part record: **claim**, **specific observation/data**, and **reasoning that links them**. In physical science, include measured quantities and units; in life science, identify the organism/system; in Earth science, cite the map, model, or time evidence. These are evidence practices in the NYS standards, not a reported Ditmas assignment or a substitute experiment.
